scene: A runaway slave has thrown his arms around the altar of Artemis and claimed asylum. His master stands at the temple steps with two men and a rope.

choices.label: Invoke the goddess's protection and negotiate his sale to another house
choices.resultText: The master rages and accepts a price. The slave goes to a gentler house. The altar has done what altars are for.

choices.label: Tell the master to wait until the man lets go
choices.resultText: He lets go on the third day, from thirst. The master pays a fee for the temple's patience. You wash the altar afterward.

scene: Lightning splits the great oak by the sacred spring. The chora is at the temple by noon, asking what it means.

choices.label: Read it as a warning and call a fast
choices.resultText: Three days without meat. Nothing terrible happens, which is taken as proof the fast worked.

choices.label: Consecrate the split oak as a new shrine
choices.resultText: Ligurians and Greeks both leave offerings at the split. The temple collects them, and is thoughtful about whose gods are answering.

scene: The temple treasury holds old votive gold no one has counted in a generation. The roof needs work; so, privately, does your house.

choices.label: Melt what the roof needs and account for every gram
choices.resultText: A new roof, an honest ledger, and a treasury lighter by exactly what the priests can defend.

choices.label: Melt a little more than the roof needs
choices.resultText: The roof is fine. Your house is finer. An old sacristan counts what was there, and tells someone who tells someone.

scene: A trader offers the temple a lock of hair from the Ephesian Artemis's own priestess, the one who came with the founders. It is beautifully boxed and probably goat.

choices.label: Buy it and display it
choices.resultText: Pilgrims come to see it. The offerings pay for the box within a year. You do not open the box.

choices.label: Refuse it publicly
choices.resultText: He sells it to Olbia's temple. Olbia's pilgrimage doubles. You are right, and poorer.

scene: A spring in the temple precinct has cured, the story goes, a Gaulish woman's blindness. Now there is a queue, and a question of whether to charge.

choices.label: Let the water be free
choices.resultText: The queue grows. So do the offerings, left unasked. The goddess, it seems, prefers not to invoice.

choices.label: Charge an obol a cup, for the temple
choices.resultText: The queue shrinks to those who can pay. The cures, oddly, shrink with it.

scene: A Carthaginian captain wants to offer a silver bull to Artemis for a safe passage. He calls her Tanit. The temple has never taken Punic silver.

choices.label: Accept the bull and call her by her name
choices.resultText: The bull stands in the treasury. The old families ask whose goddess it honors. You say: the one who answers.

choices.label: Refuse; Artemis is not Tanit
choices.resultText: He offers it to the sea instead. The old families praise you. The sea, presumably, is pleased.

scene: Roman envoys ask to sacrifice at Artemis's altar by their own rite, with covered heads. The sacristans are scandalized.

choices.label: Allow it, and learn the rite
choices.resultText: Covered heads, a pig, Latin. The goddess takes it. You now know more about Rome than the council does.

choices.label: Insist on the Greek rite
choices.resultText: They uncover their heads and manage. Later, one of them tells you Rome will have this temple's goddess in Rome one day. He is right.

scene: A Kleitos daughter is to be initiated, and the family wants the rite shortened for her health. The rite has never been shortened.

choices.label: The full rite, slowly
choices.resultText: She faints once and finishes. Her father does not forgive you and her mother sends a gift every year.

choices.label: Shorten it and say nothing
choices.resultText: A quick rite, a grateful House. The old sacristan counts the verses and says nothing, loudly.

scene: The temple's sacred snake has died. The sacristans want a new one from Epidauros; a Gaulish hand says the hills have snakes just as holy.

choices.label: Send for one from Epidauros
choices.resultText: Six months, one snake, a great deal of ceremony at the docks. It bites a sacristan on arrival, which is taken as auspicious.

choices.label: Take a snake from the hills
choices.resultText: A hill-snake in the holy basket. It thrives. Ligurians start coming to the temple to see their snake in Greek company.

scene: A rich widow brings a dream: a ship, a wolf, and her dead husband saying a name. She will pay for a reading and pay more for the right one.

choices.label: Read it honestly
choices.resultText: The name is her steward's. She pays the fee and dismisses him. You did not tell her to; the dream did.

choices.label: Read it as she wants
choices.resultText: The name is her son's. She is comforted and generous. The steward keeps stealing.

scene: Fever in the lower city. The people want a great sacrifice; the physicians want the temple to say 'boil the water' with the goddess's authority.

choices.label: Sacrifice, and proclaim the physicians' rule as the goddess's will
choices.resultText: The altars smoke and the water boils. The fever breaks in a month. Both parties claim it.

choices.label: Sacrifice only; physic is not the temple's
choices.resultText: The altars smoke. The fever breaks in two months. The physicians say what they think of the temple, in the agora.

scene: A lead curse-tablet is found buried by the temple gate, naming a councilor and asking Artemis to rot his ships. The hand is a citizen's.

choices.label: Burn it and say nothing
choices.resultText: Lead in the brazier. The councilor's ships sail fine. The citizen, months later, comes to the temple with a very large offering and a look.

choices.label: Take it to the Ephors
choices.resultText: A trial, a fine, a family shamed. The goddess's gate is clean and nobody buries anything there again. They bury it elsewhere.

scene: The Artemisia's accounts are short by a chest of silver. The choregos is a Timon and the shortfall is between his House and the temple's honor.

choices.label: Audit him publicly
choices.resultText: The chest turns up in a Timon storeroom, 'mislaid'. The festival is paid for. House Timon prays at Apollo's temple now.

choices.label: Let him make it good quietly, with interest
choices.resultText: The chest returns with a second, smaller chest. The temple's honor is intact and its ledger is creative.

scene: The hunters' guild wants a festival hunt in Artemis's name, with the goddess's blessing on their spears. The last one killed a boy.

choices.label: Bless it and ride with them
choices.resultText: Two boars and no boys. The feast is under the goddess's eye and the hunters' guild owes you the first haunch every year.

choices.label: Refuse; the goddess hunts, men pray
choices.resultText: They hunt without the blessing. Nobody dies. They do not ask again, and the haunches go elsewhere.

scene: The mother temple at Ephesos sends for the yearly tribute, doubled, citing a new roof. Massalia's temple has a roof of its own to think about.

choices.label: Pay it in full
choices.resultText: Ephesos writes a letter of thanks that is read at the Artemisia. Massalia's roof leaks another year, gloriously.

choices.label: Send half and a letter about roofs
choices.resultText: Ephesos accepts half and does not write. Massalia's roof is fixed. The goddess, you decide, has two houses and one sense of humor.

scene: A temple slave has borne a child. By custom the child is the goddess's. By decency it is hers.

choices.label: Free the child at the altar
choices.resultText: A free child in a slave's arms, under the goddess. The sacristans mutter about precedent. The mother does not.

choices.label: Register the child as the temple's
choices.resultText: Custom kept. The child will sweep the same floor as its mother. You see them both, every day.

scene: The senior priestess and you disagree, publicly, on the order of the procession. She has the older claim; you have the Archon's ear.

choices.label: Yield to her
choices.resultText: She walks first. She is gracious in victory and, for a year, an ally, which is worth more than the order of a procession.

choices.label: Take it to the Archon
choices.resultText: You walk first. She walks second, and remembers it in every rite you share for the rest of your lives.

scene: A Gaulish priest, a real one, asks to sacrifice to Artemis at her altar, saying she is Arduinna of the boar and the moon. He may be right.

choices.label: Let him sacrifice, and watch
choices.resultText: A boar, a knife, a hymn in Gaulish. The goddess, you are fairly sure, recognized it. So did the Palaioi, watching from the steps.

choices.label: Refuse him the altar
choices.resultText: He sacrifices in the hills instead, to Arduinna. Ligurians who used to come to your altar go to the hills that day.

scene: The Archon comes in secret to ask the goddess whether to arm the convoy. He wants a yes. The liver, when you look, is ambiguous.

choices.label: Tell him the liver is ambiguous
choices.resultText: He arms the convoy anyway, and says the goddess approved. You say nothing. The convoy is fine.

choices.label: Give him his yes
choices.resultText: He arms the convoy and credits the goddess and you. The convoy is fine. You look at livers differently now.

scene: A harbor orphan has been sleeping under the temple portico and sweeping it before the sacristans wake. He asks nothing. He is clearly asking.

choices.label: Take him as an acolyte
choices.resultText: He learns the hymns faster than the citizens' sons. In ten years he is the best sacristan the temple has had.

choices.label: Send him to the harbor guild for work
choices.resultText: He hauls rope. He still sweeps the portico at dawn, before work, and you stop being able to look at the portico.

scene: The sacred embassy to Delphi needs a priest of Artemis to walk with it and speak for the city before Apollo. It is an honor and four months.

choices.label: Walk with the theoria
choices.resultText: The rock, the smoke, the god's verse. You speak Massalia's name in the sanctuary, and the god, through the priestess, says something about wolves.

choices.label: Send your best acolyte
choices.resultText: He returns with the verse and a new gravity. The wolves, he says, are ours to interpret. You have four months of temple politics to show for it.

scene: A tailed star. The lower city is on the temple steps by dusk, some praying, some selling amulets, one shouting that the goddess has abandoned the city.

choices.label: Speak calmly and name it a sign of change, not ruin
choices.resultText: The crowd goes home. Change comes, as it does. You are quoted as having foreseen it.

choices.label: Order a great purification and let the fear feed the altars
choices.resultText: Nine days of smoke and offering. The treasury is full and the city is exhausted. The star fades on its own, as they do.

scene: A Gaulish grove-keeper who has watched you heal offers to teach you the plants his people keep secret, on condition you never sell the knowledge.

choices.label: Learn, and swear
choices.resultText: Seven plants, seven seasons, and a way of reading the smoke of a burning herb that tells you more than a liver ever has.

choices.label: Decline; a Greek priest does not swear to a Gaul
choices.resultText: He teaches a Philon physician instead. The physician's cures are talked about. Yours are prayed for.

scene: The senior priestess is dying and names you, before the whole college, as the one who will speak for the goddess at the Artemisia. The college is silent; the silence has an edge.

choices.label: Accept, kneeling
choices.resultText: You speak for the city's patron at her festival. Every word you say from the steps is now the goddess's, and every enemy you have is now hers.

choices.label: Decline in favor of an elder
choices.resultText: An elder speaks. He speaks well. The college remembers who was named and who stepped aside, and both are useful.

scene: A citizen marrying a Ligurian girl asks you to bless the marriage at Artemis's altar. The bride's people will attend, with their own priest.

choices.label: Bless it, both priests at the altar
choices.resultText: Two priests, one altar, a bride who cries in two languages. The old families do not attend and hear all about it.

choices.label: Refuse the altar to a mixed rite
choices.resultText: They marry at the western gate. The Ligurian priest blesses it alone, and the couple's first child is named for him.

scene: At the Artemisia, a drunk citizen of a great House vomits in the procession's path. The procession is yours to halt or to continue.

choices.label: Halt, purify the path, resume
choices.resultText: Twenty minutes of salt and prayer with the whole city watching. The House sends a silver bowl in the morning, and the citizen, sober, to carry it.

choices.label: Step round it and continue
choices.resultText: The procession flows on. The old sacristans note the unpurified stones. The House notes the mercy.

scene: A trader asks the temple for a loan against his cargo, at the goddess's rate. His cargo is silphium and his ship is old.

choices.label: Lend at the sacred rate
choices.resultText: The ship returns. The loan returns with it, and a jar of silphium for the altar that is not, strictly, interest.

choices.label: Refuse; the goddess is not a bank
choices.resultText: He borrows from a Punic factor at a Punic rate. The ship returns. So does the factor, for his percentage.

scene: In a year of blight the old families ask for the old rite: a beggar led round the walls and driven out with fig-branches, carrying the city's ill-luck.

choices.label: Perform the rite, and see the beggar fed after
choices.resultText: Fig-branches, hymns, a man walking out of the gate with the city's bad year on his back and a purse in his hand. The blight lifts. It would have anyway. Perhaps.

choices.label: Refuse; the goddess does not want a beggar
choices.resultText: No rite. The blight lifts in its own time. The old families are sure it lifted later than it would have.

scene: The fish in the temple pool, sacred and uncounted, have been counted by a sacristan, and there are fewer. Someone is eating the goddess's carp.

choices.label: Sit the pool by night and catch the thief
choices.resultText: A heron. You sit three nights for a heron. You tell the sacristan it was a heron and he is not sure whether to be relieved.

choices.label: Pronounce a curse on the thief from the steps
choices.resultText: The curse is dramatic and effective: three families bring guilt-offerings for fish they did not eat. The heron continues.

scene: An Archon has died in office. His House wants a funeral beyond the sumptuary law; the Ephors want the law kept. Both look to the temple.

choices.label: Keep the law, and make the plain rite magnificent
choices.resultText: A plain bier, a great silence, a hymn sung by the whole city. The House is furious and then, hearing the hymn, is not.

choices.label: Bend the law for an Archon
choices.resultText: Hired mourners, incense from Arabia, a bier of cedar. The Ephors fine the House, which pays laughing, and the temple, which does not.

scene: The college of priests, which does not love a colleague more followed than itself, votes that the temple's debt shall be borne by its most prominent member.

choices.label: Pay the share
choices.resultText: The debt is paid in your name. The college is grateful in the way colleges are, which is quietly and not for long.

choices.label: Refuse the levy from the steps
choices.resultText: The college pays it from the treasury and remembers who would not. Your name is left off the next three rites.

scene: The harvest failed, and the city remembers that you read the spring omens and called them good. Nobody blames the weather.

choices.label: Fund a great rite of apology
choices.resultText: Every altar in the city smokes at your expense. The city forgives the goddess. It takes longer with you.

choices.label: Stand by the reading
choices.resultText: The omens were good, you say, and the harvest was a different question. Nobody agrees, and everyone repeats it.
